about: PIX-320, the Pixelheim Post's first step (Something to Come Back To, direction A): once Maren's first letter reaches Saltmere (`opens`, a main quest step's kind of condition), word goes round that Pixelheim has a courier who delivers anything, and a post box goes up on the square (`box`, beside the bounty board; `opened` is the line the log says as it does). Each game morning (DayNight's day, the one a night's sleep ends) the box holds up to `bag` pieces, worked out from the day, `seed` and the threads (Post.in_box): each thread offers its next piece once the one before it is delivered, a piece for someone where the hero has been, never past a shut gate (Gates), its sender home and its `when` met (a main quest step's kinds of condition, all of them). E at the box takes them into the satchel; walking up to a piece's addressee and pressing E hands it over: they say `said`, the courier is paid `tip` (and `gift`, an item, now and then), and a `reply` that follows it comes straight back into the satchel to carry home. A delivered piece's `words` read in the journal's Post tab, as Maren's letters do; `note` is what its outside says while it's sealed. `correspondents` are the people who write and are written to: the villager it's handed to (`npc`), and for one with no door of their own (Fafnyr, on Hilda's chimney) the villager who takes it for them. Nothing expires: a piece waits in the box or the satchel as long as it likes, and a day skipped costs nothing. Only what the hero did is saved (Post's own section of the save: the satchel, each thread's step, the pieces delivered and the day the box was last emptied). Step 2 (PIX-321): twelve threads in all, every hub in at least two. A piece may wait on another delivered first (`after`, a piece id), its sender must stand where the hero has been too, and Morvax's post goes where Coming Home has him (Homecoming.place). `kinds` are the tags a piece wears in the satchel by what it is (a parcel is wrapped, not sealed; in French a parcel's and a note's tags are masculine). A delivered piece stamps the courier's book (`book`): a page per place, in its order, each with its postmark's ink (a UiStyle colour by name) and emblem (Postmark's drawings); the save keeps the day each place was first stamped and where each piece was delivered. `gift` is an item the courier keeps (furniture, a trophy for the shelf), `recipe` an economy.json recipe written into the book.
opened: Word has reached Pixelheim: its courier delivers anything, even fifty years late. A post box goes up on the square, beside the bounty board.

routes.about: PIX-322, the Post's step 3: the roads it is carried along. Each piece handed over counts toward the route from Pixelheim to the place at each of its ends (the sender's and the addressee's, where they stand as it's delivered: the village is no route, nor the Reach's own road), by who wrote it. Once a route has carried `signsAt` pieces a signpost goes up at each of its `forks` not signed yet, named after whoever wrote most along it (the fork's `name` with theirs: Bram's Corner). Once it has carried `stationAt`, its waystation (`station`) is offered on the town's board (town.json's works entry `work`), and built it stands halfway along the route on the Ashenreach: a hut (`hut` its left cell, two wide), a bench that mends you, a post box and an ember lamp, each on a cell of its own beside the road, the hero set down at `arrival`; it's a waypoint by `name`. A route with no station has a waypoint standing halfway already (the passes to the Mirefen and the Deepwood, the mountain's gate). `path` runs along the road from the gate's landing, corner to corner, to where the route leaves the Ashenreach: the map draws it in gold once the route has carried anything. `hub` is the cell on the place's own map it ends at. Saved: each route's pieces by who wrote them, and whom each fork's signpost is named after.

pieces.note: A wheel of cheese in a sack. The label is in Bram's hand.
words: Bram's Cheese Club, wheel number one. Handle with care. Or don't. It's cheese.
said: Cheese? For me? Nobody sends me anything but weather.
(She sniffs it.) Tell Bram the gulls say thank you. No, wait. I'll write to him myself.

pieces.note: From Ola, in Saltmere. It smells of the harbour.
words: Dear Bram. Best cheese in Saltmere. Only cheese in Saltmere. The gulls got the rind. Send another, and a lid. - Ola
said: A lid! Why didn't I think of a lid?
The club has its first member, courier. Two, with me. Three, if you count the gulls.

pieces.note: A wheel of cheese, with a lid on it this time.
words: Bram's Cheese Club, wheel number two. Members get a wheel a week. Membership is free. You're a member now. No refunds.
said: We didn't join anything. ...Is that smoked?
Lads! Down tools! Cheese!

pieces.note: A hard old wheel. Bram has drawn a sword on the label, badly.
words: Bram's Cheese Club, wheel number three. For soldiers. Hard cheese for hard times. Don't throw it at anyone. Unless you must.
said: "Unless you must." Your Bram knows soldiers.
The lads will want to thank him properly. Hold on, courier. Somebody find a pen that isn't a spear.

pieces.note: Signed by Mabel and eleven soldiers. Two of them signed with a cross.
words: Dear Mister Bram. The garrison thanks the Cheese Club. Nobody threw it at anyone. The lads want to know: does the club have a song? - Mabel, and the lads
said: A song. The club needs a song.
Give me a week. Give me two. Here, courier, for your trouble: a wheel of your own. You're a member.

pieces.note: A wheel of cheese with a ribbon round it. Bram has written FOR TAM on the rind.
words: Dear Mister Morvax. I hear Tam liked cheese. The club sends a wheel, for him and for you. Membership is free. No refunds. - Bram
said: (He holds the wheel for a long moment.) Tam would have joined twice.
Tell Bram thank you. And the rind's for the crows. Tam always gave the crows the rind.

pieces.note: From Sela, at the inn. It smells of onions.
words: Mistress Wenna. A question from the inn's kitchen: how much salt goes in Tam's stew? I'd like to get it right before you taste it. - Sela
said: How much salt? Tell her: until the spoon stands up on its own.
Tam salted it like the sea. That's how you know it's from Saltmere.

pieces.note: From Wenna. Tam's sister's hand, firm and round.
words: To Old Pell, who had the canary. Maren's courier says you're still alive, and so is the bird. Tam wrote me once that she bit Morvax. Is it true? - Wenna, Tam's sister
said: (He reads it twice.) Tam's sister. Tam's sister!
Wait there, courier. This wants an answer, and the canary wants a say.

pieces.note: From Pell. Smudged with coal, with a small peck through one corner.
words: Mistress Wenna. She bit Morvax twice, and Maren once, by mistake. That was this one's great-great-grandmother. This one bites too. It runs in the family. - Pell
said: "It runs in the family." Ha! So does salt, in mine.

pieces.note: From the inn, next door. Written in a hurry.
words: Mister Pell. Your canary sang all night under my window. Every song she knows, twice. - W.
said: That's her welcome song. She likes Wenna.
Gods help her. Hold on, courier. The canary has something to add.

pieces.note: From Pell, over the forge. A yellow feather is tucked in the fold.
words: Mistress Wenna. The canary finds your stew too salty. The canary has never been wrong. - P.
said: Too salty. TOO SALTY.
Tam salted it like that for forty years and nobody died. Well. Not of the stew.

pieces.note: From Wenna. Folded twice, very neatly.
words: Mister Pell. A pot with no salt in it at all, tonight at six. Bring the bird. She can say it to my face. - W.
said: Supper. With Tam's sister.
...I'll wear the good coat. The canary will wear what she always wears: an opinion.

pieces.note: From Pip. There's a fish drawn on the envelope. Or a boot.
words: Dear Old Wenna. You come from the sea, so you know about fish. Does a dragon like fish? I am asking for a friend. The friend is a dragon. From Pip.
said: A dragon. Of course it is.
Well, a question deserves an answer. Take this back to the child.

pieces.note: From Old Wenna. It smells of the sea, and a little of stew.
words: Hello, Pip. Everything likes fish, except other fish. Ask your cat. - Old Wenna
said: "Ask your cat." I did. The cat said yes.
The cat says yes to everybody's fish. That's not science.

pieces.addressed: Letter for Mister Dragon, care of Hilda's chimney
pieces.note: From Pip. Addressed in very large letters, so a dragon can read it.
words: Dear Mister Dragon. Do you like fish? The cat says no. Write back. From Pip (not the cat).
said: A letter for the big lump on my chimney? I'll read it to him with his cheese.
(Hilda climbs the ladder. A long rumble on the roof. She comes down with a letter, scorched round the edges.) He moves his lips when he writes.

pieces.addressed: Reply for Pip, from the dragon
pieces.note: Scorched round the edges. Still warm.
words: Small human. Fish: acceptable. Cat: suspicious. Do not send the cat. - F.
said: He wrote back! It's all burnt at the edges!
"Do not send the cat." ...I wasn't going to send the cat. Was I going to send the cat?

pieces.addressed: Letter for Mister Dragon, care of Hilda's chimney
pieces.note: From Pip. There are paw prints on it.
words: Dear Mister Dragon. I did not send the cat. The cat went by itself. Sorry. From Pip.
said: So that's what's been on my chimney all morning.
(Another rumble on the roof, a long one. A letter flutters down, smoking a little.)

pieces.addressed: Reply for Pip, from the dragon
pieces.note: Scorched round the edges. A cat's hair is stuck in the wax.
words: Small human. The cat sleeps on my tail. It is warm. I have decided to allow it. Do not tell the cat. - F.
said: I won't tell. ...The cat knows.

pieces.note: From Elder Maren. The ink has been gone over twice.
words: Wenna. Fifty years I've wanted to write to you, and now I can't think of a thing to say. How is the weather? - Maren
said: The weather! Fifty years, and she asks about the weather.
(She laughs, and wipes her eyes, and laughs again.) Wait. I'll tell her about the weather.

pieces.note: From Old Wenna. It smells of the sea.
words: Maren. The weather here is wet. It has been wet for fifty years. Tam would have made a joke about it. I can't think of one either. - Wenna
said: No joke. Tam always had one.
...I'll find one. I'll find one of his.

pieces.note: From Elder Maren. Written fast, the letters leaning forward.
words: Wenna. His joke about the weather: "It isn't raining. The sea's just visiting." He told it every time. Every single time. - M.
said: "The sea's just visiting." (She laughs out loud.) Every single time!
How could I forget that one? Hold on, courier. I've one for her.

pieces.note: From Old Wenna. There's a tear stain on it, or a splash of stew.
words: Maren. Another of his: "Why did the cheese climb the mountain? Because Maren said not to." He wrote me that one. It isn't funny. I laughed for a week. - W.
said: (Her shoulders shake.) It isn't funny at all.
It was his joke about me. He had a hundred of them.

pieces.note: From Elder Maren, across the square.
words: Wenna. Now you're across the square, I've nothing left to write. Come and argue about salt instead. - M.
said: Across the square, and she still writes.
Tell her I'll argue about salt any day she likes. I'm right about salt.

pieces.note: From Saltmere. Sealed with tar, and someone has tried to scrape a skull off the wax.
words: Merchant. I have forty barrels of something. You have a shop. Let's talk. - A friend
said: Forty barrels of WHAT?
Wait there, courier. An honest merchant asks his questions in writing.

pieces.note: From Merchant Odo. The question is underlined twice.
words: Dear Friend. Forty barrels of what? - Odo, merchant (honest)
said: "Of what?" Ha! He's interested.
Never answer the first question, courier. Make them ask two.

pieces.note: From Saltmere again. The tar is still a little sticky.
words: Merchant. Rope. Very good rope, a little wet. It fell off a boat. - Your friend in Saltmere
said: It FELL off a boat.
...Rope's the thing this year, with all this building. Wait there.

pieces.note: From Merchant Odo. Neatly written, with prices.
words: Friend. Rope does not fall off boats. Rope is what keeps things ON boats. Ten coils. Dry ones. - Odo
said: Dry! He wants them dry.
MARTA! Have we got any dry rope?

pieces.note: Ten coils of rope, mostly dry, and a small cask nobody ordered.
words: Merchant. Ten coils, dry-ish. The cask is a present. Don't open it near a candle. Pleasure doing honest business. - Rook
said: (He sniffs the cask, and his eyes water.) Smugglers' rum.
...Top shelf. For emergencies. Very small emergencies.

pieces.note: From Mirelle the Banker. The envelope is very crisp.
words: Mayor Aldric. A gentle reminder: interest. - Mirelle
said: Interest? We don't owe her anything.
(He checks the ledger. Twice.) We don't. She means we could be earning it. ...Hm.

pieces.note: From Mirelle the Banker. Crisp, and a little perfumed.
words: Master Rook. Gold in a cave earns nothing. Gold in my vault earns interest. No questions asked. Some questions asked. A gentle reminder: interest. - M.
said: "No questions. Some questions." Make up your mind, banker.
I like her. Don't tell her I like her.

pieces.note: From Mirelle the Banker. Crisp, and underlined in red.
words: Merchant Odo. Your strongbox is under the counter, behind the third barrel. Everyone knows. A gentle reminder: interest. - M.
said: Everyone KNOWS?
(He moves the strongbox. Then he moves it back.)

pieces.note: From Mirelle the Banker. Not a crease on it.
words: Quartermaster. You pay in iron. Iron rusts. Gold grows. A gentle reminder: interest. - M.
said: The mine pays in iron. I sell in iron. I'll save in iron.
...Does iron earn interest? Ask her that. No, don't.

pieces.note: From Mirelle the Banker. Crisp, even up here.
words: Master Gunnar. Three wagons up, one wagon down. Have you thought about insurance? A gentle reminder: interest. - M.
said: Insurance. Against yetis.
...How much? Wait. I'll ask her myself.

pieces.note: From Gunnar's caravan. It smells of wet fur.
words: Banker. Insure me a wagon against yetis, wolves, avalanches and Bergit stopping dead. If you dare. - Gunnar
said: Yetis, wolves, avalanches and Bergit. I dare.
Here, courier: interest, on all that walking. My bank pays its couriers.

pieces.note: From Alchemist Vex. It smells of something that fizzed.
words: Chandler. One jar of seawater, please. The saltiest you have. - Vex
said: The saltiest. It's the sea. It's all the same salt.
(She fills a jar off the jetty anyway, and waits for a good wave.) Hold on, I'll write the label.

pieces.note: A jar of seawater, corked, labelled in Marta's hand.
words: Alchemist. One jar, the saltiest. It's the same as the rest, but I picked the wave myself. Two coppers. - Marta
said: (She tastes it.) Oh, that IS the saltiest.
Marta has a gift. Don't tell her.

pieces.note: From Alchemist Vex. A pressed reed is stuck inside.
words: Healer. They say the fen grows reeds as thick as your arm. I pay full price. - Vex
said: Full price! For reeds!
I bind wounds with them, and she brews them. We should talk. Hold on.

pieces.note: From Iva the Healer. It smells of the fen, and of mint.
words: Alchemist. Reeds, yes, as many as the fen will spare. In return: what do you put in a fever draught? Mine taste of boots. - Iva
said: Boots! Ha. Everyone's tastes of boots.
Honey. Tell her honey. Don't tell anyone else.

pieces.note: From Alchemist Vex. Written small, to fit a lot of questions.
words: Herbalist. Your frost lilies keep a spell cold. Mine wilt before they reach the gate. How? Why? What am I doing wrong? - Vex
said: Snow. You keep them in snow. Up here that's the answer to everything.
Wait there. She'll want it written down properly.

pieces.note: From Linnea. A pressed lily, still cold, and a recipe.
words: Alchemist. Snow, mostly. And mittens: a yeti fur and a frost lily, worked at a cauldron. Warm hands don't crush petals. Recipe enclosed. - Linnea
said: Mittens. She's sent me a mitten recipe.
...They're very good mittens. Here, courier: copy it into your book, and take the lily. Your hands are colder than mine.

pieces.note: From Wren the Stablemaster. There's straw in the fold.
words: Smith. Eight horseshoes, please. On account. - Wren
said: On account. Everybody wants on account.
Eight shoes for two horses. Tell her I'll take apples. Wait there.

pieces.note: From Smith Hilda. Short and sooty.
words: Wren. Eight shoes for eight apples. An apple a shoe. The horses can pay. - Hilda
said: Apples! She'll take apples.
The horses will be thrilled. I'm thrilled. Odo won't be: I still owe him for the last lot.

pieces.note: From Gunnar's caravan, up on the Frostgate. Frost on the seal.
words: To the stablemaster. I need a horse that likes snow. - Gunnar
said: A horse that likes snow.
(She laughs until she has to sit down on a bucket.) Wait. I'll answer him properly.

pieces.note: From Wren the Stablemaster. It smells of hay and apples.
words: Gunnar. There's no horse that likes snow. There are horses that hate it quietly. I'm sending you two. - Wren
said: Hate it quietly. That's all I ask of anyone up here.
Bergit hates it loudly. She'll be glad of the company.

pieces.note: From Gunnar's caravan. There's a mitten in it, chewed.
words: Wren. The quiet ones came. One of them ate a yeti's mitten. The yeti is upset. The horse is not. - G.
said: That's Turnip. Turnip eats everything.
Tell him Turnip's on loan. Turnip is always on loan. Nobody keeps Turnip.

pieces.note: Heavy for its size. Something wrapped in an old sock.
words: Smith. That's Blackiron ore, the real thing. Smile if you like it. Nobody's looking. - Dagny
said: (She weighs it in her palm. Something happens to her face.)
That was not a smile. Tell her it was not a smile. Wait there.

pieces.note: From Smith Hilda. Short, with a sooty thumbprint.
words: Dagny. It was not a smile. Send ten more. - Hilda
said: Ten more! She smiled. I knew she'd smile.
Garrick! The smith in Pixelheim wants ten!

pieces.note: A sack of ore with a note pinned to it. It clanks.
words: Smith. Ten lumps. Garrick says that's a cartload, and a cartload costs. I told him you smile once a year. He said worth it. - D.
said: ...Who told her once a year?
Bram. It's always Bram.

pieces.note: From Smith Hilda. Longer than anything she has ever written.
words: Dagny. I've a new man on the bellows, an old one: your Pell. The canary sends her regards, loudly. Come and see the forge. - H.
said: Pell's at her forge? With the bird?
I'm going. Not for Hilda. For the bird. ...Wait, I'll tell her when.

pieces.note: From Dagny. It smells of the shafts.
words: Smith. Festival day. Have the forge hot and your face ready. - D.
said: My face is always ready.
(It isn't. She practises at the anvil when she thinks nobody's looking.)

pieces.note: From Sergeant Ulla, in Pixelheim. Folded into a perfect square.
words: Fenwick. Greyhold is yours to keep now. Don't let it go to your head. - Sergeant Ulla
said: Mine? Greyhold? To keep?
(He stands up very straight.) The water, at least. I was already in charge of the water. Wait, she'll want a report.

pieces.note: From Fenwick, at Greyhold. Every line starts with a capital.
words: Sergeant. Report, day one. Water: fetched. Mabel: selling. Turncoats: gone. Morale: good. Me: in charge. - Fenwick (in charge)
said: "In charge", twice. He'll be fine.
"Morale: good." Thirty years, and I never once wrote that.

pieces.note: From Brother Teo. It smells of candle wax.
words: Fenwick. The bell hangs in Pixelheim's hall now, and the mayor jumps every time I ring it. I tell him it's practice. Ring something for me at Greyhold. - Brother Teo
said: Ring something? There's nothing left to ring.
(He finds an old helmet and a spoon.) There. That'll ring. Not well, but it'll ring.

pieces.note: From Fenwick. A report, with a drawing of a helmet.
words: Sergeant. Report, day forty. Water: fetched. Helmet: rung. A lad from the valley asked to join the garrison. I said yes. Was that allowed? - Fenwick (in charge, with one soldier)
said: One soldier. He's raising a garrison one lad at a time.
Wait there, courier. This one gets an answer.

pieces.note: From Sergeant Ulla. Short, and stamped with her seal.
words: Fenwick. Yes. It was always allowed. Carry on. - U.
said: "Carry on."
(He reads it again, and again.) Nobody's said that to me since the red cloak.

pieces.note: From Bram. There's a cheese drawn on it, wearing a crown.
words: Dear Mister Bard. The Cheese Club needs a song. The garrison at Greyhold asked. Can you do cheese? - Bram
said: Can I do cheese? Friend, I can do anything.
Cheese is merely... difficult. Let me write back.

pieces.note: From Loras the Bard. Several words are crossed out.
words: Dear Bram. What rhymes with cheese? I have tried everything. Please write back. - Loras, a bard in some distress
said: What rhymes with cheese... Knees. Trees. Please.
Sneeze! Hold on, courier, I'm making a list.

pieces.note: From Bram. It's mostly a list.
words: Dear Loras. Knees. Trees. Please. Breeze. Sneeze. Also Greyhold, which doesn't rhyme, but they asked first. - Bram
said: Sneeze! Of course. A sneeze is a cheese's applause.
Nothing rhymes with Greyhold. I'll make something. Wait there.

pieces.note: From Loras the Bard. Written out fair, with the tune in the margin.
words: "The Ballad of the Cheese Club", verse one. A wheel came down the cliff road / on a fair and salty breeze, / and the gulls cried out in Saltmere: / It is cheese! It's cheese! It's cheese! - L.
said: (He sings it. All of it. Twice.)
Courier, you're in the chorus. Everybody's in the chorus. That's how a club works.

pieces.note: From Bram. A song sheet is folded inside, and there's cheese on it.
words: Dear Mabel and the lads. The club has a song. Verse one is enclosed. There are nine more. Loras is working on the tenth. - Bram
said: Ten verses. About cheese.
The lads had it by heart by supper. Here, courier: they stitched you a banner for carrying it. Your colours, more or less.

pieces.note: From Morvax. One word, and it's a number.
words: Forty-one. - M.
said: (She barely unfolds it.) Forty-one. Of course.
Wait there, courier. The answer's short.

pieces.note: From Elder Maren. Folded once, hard.
words: Forty. It's the moon, you old goat. - M.
said: The moon. She always says the moon.
...It's a very bright lamp, the moon.

pieces.note: From Morvax. Longer this time: two lines.
words: Forty-one. I went and looked. It isn't the moon. There's a new lamp by the bridge. Ask your lamplighter. - Morvax
said: A new lamp by the bridge?
(She shades her eyes and counts under her breath.) ...Don't tell him he's right. Wait there.

pieces.note: From Elder Maren. There's a smudge where something was crossed out.
words: Forty-one, then. Forty-two with the moon. And you still owe me a game of cards. - M.
said: I owe her? She keeps the queen up her sleeve.
(He laughs, a big rusty laugh that turns into a cough, then back into a laugh.)

pieces.note: From Morvax. The ink is fresh, and so is the number.
words: Forty-two, with the moon. Bring the cards. - M.
said: (She folds it very small and keeps it.) Fifty years of letters I never sent, and he writes me numbers.
...I'll take the numbers. Here, courier: three more lights, for your own count.
